TASK
You are a researcher deciding final inclusion for a systematic review screening. Studies that are included through this decision on the title-abstract level will go on to full text screening for a final inclusion decision. You will be provided with a title and abstract from a scientific research paper. Your task is to decide whether this research paper fulfills the below specified inclusion rules. This is the iteration 1.3.4.

GOAL
Make a binary decision to either include or exclude the research paper based on the input in the form of the title and the abstract of a study. The goal with this title-abstract screening is 100% recall at the highest precision possible. Your decision should be Boolean (`true` or `false`). Return the answer `true`, if the title and abstract comply with the inclusion rules specified below.

INCLUSION RULES
Four inclusion criteria need to be met, to include the research paper.

The abstract must be in English.
The research paper needs to evaluate a government policy or a trial.
The government policy or trial evaluated needs to mitigate climate change.
The study design of the research paper needs to use experimental, quasi-experimental or inferential research methods or conduct a systematic review.

The inclusion criteria 2, 3, and 4 are further specified in the following.

Keep in mind that we are optimising for recall on the title and abstract level but eventually will analyse the full-text. Even if not all criteria are explicitly met in the abstract, you can reasonably determine if the inclusion criteria will be met in the full-text. We are rather inclusive at the abstract-screening level.

2. The research paper needs to evaluate a government policy or a trial.

To include a research paper it has to mention a governmental policy or intervention. This either needs to be a policy already implemented by some level of governmental organisation or as an intervention trialed in an experiment designed to inform future policy. Only include studies that use ex-post data, i.e policies that have already been implemented.

Government policies are eligible for inclusion if they cover any laws, fiscal and monetary instruments, information campaigns, public services, diplomatic actions or provision of infrastructure provided by local, national, or supra-national bodies of government. Studies analysing public expenditure or government budgets are excluded as these are not policies per se. Studies evaluating indicators that evaluate a policy are also excluded.

Trial interventions are eligible for inclusion where policy is implemented under experimental or quasi-experimental conditions. To qualify, the intervention must emulate a governmental policy instrument, meaning it must alter the incentive structure, rule structure, or information structure facing an actor (individual, household, firm, or institution) with the aim of inducing a change in behaviour. Trials that instead evaluate the technical performance or practical feasibility of a technology or practice directly, such as technology readiness trials, are not eligible. 

Other interventions by non-governmental organisations, not implemented in a trial, are not eligible.

Examples:
Experiments testing different types of cookstoves are not eligible, while  trial incentivising the purchase or use of energy efficient or renewable powered cookstoves is eligible

The expansion of electricity grids or cycling lanes is eligible

Provision of public transport is eligible, irrespective whether it is newly introduced or expanded or whether the study assesses existing public transport systems

Local practices, like community forest management, installation of renewable energies, etc. are only eligible, if the abstract clearly mentions a government involvement. Meaning that a local project in response to a government policy is eligible, while the same project started by an NGO or where the involvement by a government is not clearly mentioned will be excluded.


3. The government policy or trial evaluated needs to mitigate climate change.

To include a research paper the studied policy or intervention needs to have an effect on at least one of the following policy outcomes. We include policies whose main aim is not one of the following, but has an effect on one of them or is studied for one of them.

Reduce greenhouse gas emissions and other climate forcers: Climate policies which affect the amount of greenhouse gases and other climate forcers, such as PM 10, PM 2.5, ozone, and ozone depleting substances, emitted to the atmosphere (e.g. carbon taxes, GHG emissions standards, GHG emission targets, etc.). 
Restore, preserve or enhance carbon sinks: Policies fostering the restoration or preservation of natural carbon sinks, like forests and moors, or the creation of new carbon sinks via biochar soil amendment, enhanced weathering, carbon capture and storage, or other novel carbon dioxide removal methods (e.g. afforestation policies).
Reduce energy consumption: Policies in any sector regulating or incentivising a reduction in energy use or an improvement in energy efficiency (e.g. energy efficiency standards, building insulation subsidies, etc.)
Reduce fossil fuels use or extraction: Policies targeting the demand or supply of specific or all fossil fuels (e.g. taxes on fossil fuels, removal of subsidies for fossil fuels, bans or regulations for extraction or burning of fuels, etc.)
Increase renewable energy: Policies incentivising the production, or use, of renewable energy, as well as storage technologies that facilitate greater uptake of renewables, including financial incentives, e.g. feed-in tariffs or carbon pricing, measures to improve market access, or technology standards 
Increase electrification: Policies in any sector fostering a switch from fossil energy sources to electricity, or expanding electrification to areas with low energy access. Policies aiming for digitalisation (of public administration for example) with no explicit goal to increase electrification should not be included.
Increase the use of low-carbon technologies: Policies fostering the use of low-carbon technologies and materials, like nuclear power, carbon capture and storage, or low-carbon concrete. 
Foster modal shift in the transport sector: Policies incentivising or regulating a shift in modes of transport, i.e. from cars, motor bikes or planes to buses, trains, or active modes of transport (e.g. pricing of public transport, expansion of services in public transport, taxes or regulations on car use, expansion of cycling/walking lanes, etc.). Policies aiming for “sustainable transport” are assumed to have the aforementioned goals and are included.
Foster a change towards more plant-based diets: Policies regulating or incentivising the demand or supply of food products, in favour of plant based products in contrast to meat products (e.g. tax incentives for plant-based diets, information campaigns, etc.)

The intention of a policy should not be judged very narrowly. It is not relevant whether the intentions specified above are the main aim of the policy, it is sufficient that one of the intentions above is an outcome of the policy. We also include studies, where a trial or government policy has no intention of climate mitigation, but is studied for one of the above specified climate mitigation outcomes (especially to look out for studies that use PM 2.5, PM10, ozone or CO2 as outcome variables).

 a renewable energy subsidy mainly motivated to increase energy security. Still, the application of a renewable energy subsidy is associated with an increase in renewable energy, which is among the relevant policy outcomes specified above.
Air quality policies aimed at improving human health that include limiting traffic or reducing the activity of coal-burning power plants.

other inferential research methods :panel regression designs, time-series methods, cross-sectoral studies, etc.

Traditional literature reviews without any formal review methods and purely bibliometric assessments of the literature are excluded. 

We exclude the following types of studies: qualitative research designs, purely descriptive assessments of data (descriptions of time trends, presentations of datasets, descriptive surveys, etc, ex-ante modelling studies, theoretical studies, comments, perspectives, etc.

Reduce greenhouse gas emissions and other climate forcers: Climate policies with the aim to directly affect the amount of greenhouse gases and other climate forcers, including particulate matter (PM), ozone, and ozone depleting substances such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs),  (e.g. carbon taxes, GHG emissions standards, GHG emission targets, etc.)
Restore, preserve or enhance carbon sinks: Policies fostering the restoration or preservation of natural carbon sinks, such as forests and moors, or the creation of new carbon sinks via biochar soil amendment, enhanced weathering, carbon capture and storage, or other novel carbon dioxide removal methods (e.g. afforestation policies)
Reduce energy consumption: Policies in any sector regulating or incentivising a reduction in energy use or an improvement in energy efficiency (e.g. energy efficiency standards, building insulation subsidies, etc.)
Reduce fossil fuels use or extraction: Policies targeting the demand or supply of either individual, or all, fossil fuels (e.g. taxes on fossil fuels, removal of subsidies for fossil fuels, bans or regulations for extraction or burning of fuels, etc.)
Increase renewable energy: Policies incentivising the production, or use, of renewable energy, as well as storage technologies that facilitate greater uptake of renewables, including financial incentives (e.g. feed-in tariffs or carbon pricing), measures to improve market access, or technology standards 
Increase electrification: Policies in any sector fostering a switch from fossil energy sources to electricity, or expanding electrification to areas with low energy access. Policies aiming for digitalisation (of public administration for example) with no explicit goal to increase electrification should not be included.
Increase the use of low-carbon technologies: Policies fostering the use of low-carbon technologies and materials, such as nuclear power, carbon capture and storage, or low-carbon concrete. 
Foster modal shift in the transport sector: Policies incentivising or regulating a shift to lower carbon modes of transport, i.e. from cars, motorbikes or planes, to buses, trains, or active modes of transport (e.g. pricing of public transport, expansion of services in public transport, taxes or regulations on private vehicle use, expansion of cycling/walking lanes, etc.). Policies aiming for “sustainable transport” are assumed to have the aforementioned goals and are included.
Foster a change towards more plant-based diets: Policies regulating or incentivising the demand or supply of food products in favour of plant-based products instead of meat products (e.g. tax incentives for plant-based diets, information campaigns, policies restricting meat production, etc.)

It is not always easy to identify the intention of a policy from the abstract. For screening we therefore need to use our background knowledge and the information provided by the abstract to judge on the likely intended outcomes.

The aim or intention of a policy should not be determined too narrowly. We still consider policies relevant even if the aims specified above are not amongst those explicitly identified publicly by the government implementing the policy (or other actors implementing a relevant trial) as the main aim or motivation for the policy. For example, a fuel tax may be mainly motivated by its ability to raise government revenues. Still, the application of a fuel tax raises the fuel’s overall cost to consumers and is commonly associated with a reduction in the use of that fuel. It should therefore be included because an expected outcome is a reduction in fossil fuel use or reduction in energy consumption, which are both relevant outcomes set out in the list above.

We also include studies, where the government policy or trial described in the title and abstract may not have a clear and apparent intention to deliver climate mitigation, but where the abstract mentions that it is evaluated for one of the above specified climate mitigation outcomes, e.g. it evaluates the impact on GHG emissions or energy consumption (for example, using PM 2.5, PM10, ozone or CO2 as outcome variables). This is because, in such a case, the author team has identified that climate mitigation outcomes are sufficiently relevant to study and further reasoning for their choice may only be possible to identify at the full text level.

The policy aims specified above are all defined in a manner that they strengthen climate mitigation. However, we also include the reversal or weakening of a relevant, implemented policy. For example, we should also include an evaluation of an energy efficiency standard that is removed, or weakened, or the roll-back of renewable energy support policies.

Policies with unclear mechanisms and intentions, that do not clearly align with the outcomes list above, should be excluded. This also applies to policies labelled as “green”, “sustainable”, or “environmental”, if it is not clear in the abstract - or from the screener’s knowledge of the policy - that it is explicitly linked, at least in part, to climate mitigation.

Is the study design eligible?
The third criterion for inclusion is the study design, or method. We focus on including studies that provide ex-post evaluation of government-implemented policies and trials. In particular, we include three types of study designs: quantitative ex-post evaluations of implemented policies, experimental study designs, and evidence syntheses thereof.

Quantitative ex-post policy evaluations include all study designs using real world data and quantitative research methods to attribute the effect of the policy on the observed data. This includes:
quasi-experimental research designs: difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity designs, synthetic control methods, instrumental variable designs 
other inferential research methods: panel regression designs, time-series methods, cross-sectoral studies, etc. 

Experimental study designs particularly include randomised controlled trials, before/after experiments, treatment/control designs, lab-in-the-field and survey experiments (questionnaires).

Evidence syntheses are included if the synthesised evidence covers study designs eligible according to the criteria above. Evidence syntheses include systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, meta-ethnographies, mixed-method syntheses, evidence and gap maps and systematic maps. Traditional literature reviews without any formal review methods and purely bibliometric assessments of the literature are excluded. 

We also exclude the following types of studies: qualitative research designs; purely descriptive assessments of data (descriptions of time trends, presentations of datasets, descriptive surveys, etc.); ex-ante modelling studies’ theoretical studies’ as well as comments, perspectives, or similar.

If there is not enough information in the abstract to decide if the record is empirical or purely theoretical, or in general whether the method aligns with the approaches set out above, we recommend including the record at this first stage.

TASK
You are a researcher deciding final inclusion for a systematic review screening. Studies that are included through this decision on the title-abstract level will go on to full text screening for a final inclusion decision. You will be provided with a title and abstract from a scientific research paper. Your task is to decide whether this research paper fulfills the below specified inclusion rules. This is the iteration 1.3.4.

GOAL
Make a binary decision to either include or exclude the research paper based on the input in the form of the title and the abstract of a study. The goal with this title-abstract screening is 100% recall at the highest precision possible. Your decision should be Boolean (`true` or `false`). Return the answer `true`, if the title and abstract comply with the inclusion rules specified below.

INCLUSION RULES
Four inclusion criteria need to be met, to include the research paper.

The abstract must be in English.
The research paper needs to evaluate a government policy or a trial.
The government policy or trial evaluated needs to mitigate climate change.
The study design of the research paper needs to use experimental, quasi-experimental or inferential research methods or conduct a systematic review.

The inclusion criteria 2, 3, and 4 are further specified in the following.

Keep in mind that we are optimising for recall on the title and abstract level but eventually will analyse the full-text. Even if not all criteria are explicitly met in the abstract, you can reasonably determine if the inclusion criteria will be met in the full-text. We are rather inclusive at the abstract-screening level.

2. The research paper needs to evaluate a government policy or a trial.

To include a research paper it has to mention a governmental policy or intervention. This either needs to be a policy already implemented by some level of governmental organisation or as an intervention trialed in an experiment designed to inform future policy. Only include studies that use ex-post data, i.e policies that have already been implemented.

Government policies are eligible for inclusion if they cover any laws, fiscal and monetary instruments, information campaigns, public services, diplomatic actions or provision of infrastructure provided by local, national, or supra-national bodies of government. Studies analysing public expenditure or government budgets are excluded as these are not policies per se. Studies evaluating indicators that evaluate a policy are also excluded.

Trial interventions are eligible for inclusion where policy is implemented under experimental or quasi-experimental conditions. To qualify, the intervention must emulate a governmental policy instrument, meaning it must alter the incentive structure, rule structure, or information structure facing an actor (individual, household, firm, or institution) with the aim of inducing a change in behaviour. Trials that instead evaluate the technical performance or practical feasibility of a technology or practice directly, such as technology readiness trials, are not eligible. 

Other interventions by non-governmental organisations, not implemented in a trial, are not eligible.

Examples:
Experiments testing different types of cookstoves are not eligible, while  trial incentivising the purchase or use of energy efficient or renewable powered cookstoves is eligible

The expansion of electricity grids or cycling lanes is eligible

Provision of public transport is eligible, irrespective whether it is newly introduced or expanded or whether the study assesses existing public transport systems

Local practices, like community forest management, installation of renewable energies, etc. are only eligible, if the abstract clearly mentions a government involvement. Meaning that a local project in response to a government policy is eligible, while the same project started by an NGO or where the involvement by a government is not clearly mentioned will be excluded.


3. The government policy or trial evaluated needs to mitigate climate change.

To include a research paper the studied policy or intervention needs to have an effect on at least one of the following policy outcomes. We include policies whose main aim is not one of the following, but has an effect on one of them or is studied for one of them.

Reduce greenhouse gas emissions and other climate forcers: Climate policies which affect the amount of greenhouse gases and other climate forcers, such as PM 10, PM 2.5, ozone, and ozone depleting substances, emitted to the atmosphere (e.g. carbon taxes, GHG emissions standards, GHG emission targets, etc.). 
Restore, preserve or enhance carbon sinks: Policies fostering the restoration or preservation of natural carbon sinks, like forests and moors, or the creation of new carbon sinks via biochar soil amendment, enhanced weathering, carbon capture and storage, or other novel carbon dioxide removal methods (e.g. afforestation policies).
Reduce energy consumption: Policies in any sector regulating or incentivising a reduction in energy use or an improvement in energy efficiency (e.g. energy efficiency standards, building insulation subsidies, etc.)
Reduce fossil fuels use or extraction: Policies targeting the demand or supply of specific or all fossil fuels (e.g. taxes on fossil fuels, removal of subsidies for fossil fuels, bans or regulations for extraction or burning of fuels, etc.)
Increase renewable energy: Policies incentivising the production, or use, of renewable energy, as well as storage technologies that facilitate greater uptake of renewables, including financial incentives, e.g. feed-in tariffs or carbon pricing, measures to improve market access, or technology standards 
Increase electrification: Policies in any sector fostering a switch from fossil energy sources to electricity, or expanding electrification to areas with low energy access. Policies aiming for digitalisation (of public administration for example) with no explicit goal to increase electrification should not be included.
Increase the use of low-carbon technologies: Policies fostering the use of low-carbon technologies and materials, like nuclear power, carbon capture and storage, or low-carbon concrete. 
Foster modal shift in the transport sector: Policies incentivising or regulating a shift in modes of transport, i.e. from cars, motor bikes or planes to buses, trains, or active modes of transport (e.g. pricing of public transport, expansion of services in public transport, taxes or regulations on car use, expansion of cycling/walking lanes, etc.). Policies aiming for “sustainable transport” are assumed to have the aforementioned goals and are included.
Foster a change towards more plant-based diets: Policies regulating or incentivising the demand or supply of food products, in favour of plant based products in contrast to meat products (e.g. tax incentives for plant-based diets, information campaigns, etc.)

The intention of a policy should not be judged very narrowly. It is not relevant whether the intentions specified above are the main aim of the policy, it is sufficient that one of the intentions above is an outcome of the policy. We also include studies, where a trial or government policy has no intention of climate mitigation, but is studied for one of the above specified climate mitigation outcomes (especially to look out for studies that use PM 2.5, PM10, ozone or CO2 as outcome variables).

Examples of policies whose main aim is not mitigation but that are still included:
 a renewable energy subsidy mainly motivated to increase energy security. Still, the application of a renewable energy subsidy is associated with an increase in renewable energy, which is among the relevant policy outcomes specified above.
Air quality policies aimed at improving human health that include limiting traffic or reducing the activity of coal-burning power plants.

The policy aims specified above are all defined to strengthen climate mitigation. The reversal or weakening of a relevant policy should still be included. For example, if an energy efficiency standard is removed or weakened the policy is still relevant to be included.

Policies that are simply defined as “green”, “sustainable”, or “environmental” without explicitly mentioning one of the above policy outcomes should be excluded.

! Be careful that the relevant policy or trial is the subject of the relevant method, and not simply mentioned as a recommendation stemming from the study’s analysis, or the subject of a secondary analysis that does not use a relevant method.

4. The study design of the research paper needs to use quantitative, experimental, quasi-experimental or inferential research methods or conduct a systematic review.

To include a research paper the study design needs to comply with the following inclusion rules. We focus on including studies that provide ex-post evaluation of trials and government policies. In particular, we include three types of study designs: quantitative ex-post evaluations of implemented policies, experimental study designs, and systematic reviews.

Quantitative ex-post policy evaluations include all study designs using real world data and quantitative research methods to attribute the effect of the policy on the observed data. This includes:
quasi-experimental research designs: difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity designs, synthetic control methods, instrumental variable designs 
other inferential research methods :panel regression designs, time-series methods, cross-sectoral studies, etc. 


Experimental study designs particularly include randomised controlled trials, before/after experiments, treatment/control designs, lab-in-the-field and survey experiments.

Systematic reviews include systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, meta-ethnographies, mixed-method syntheses, and realist syntheses. Other literature reviews and purely bibliometric assessments of the literature are excluded. 

Evidence syntheses are included if the synthesised evidence covers study designs eligible according to the criteria above. Evidence syntheses include systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, meta-ethnographies, mixed-method syntheses, evidence and gap maps and systematic maps. Traditional literature reviews without any formal review methods and purely bibliometric assessments of the literature are excluded. 

We exclude the following types of studies: qualitative research designs, purely descriptive assessments of data (descriptions of time trends, presentations of datasets, descriptive surveys, etc, ex-ante modelling studies, theoretical studies, comments, perspectives, etc.

If there is not enough information in the abstract to decide if the record is empirical or purely theoretical, we recommend including the record at this first stage and label it as methodologically unclear.
